trial_name: BICKELL — Immediate vs Delayed Fluid Resuscitation in Penetrating Torso Trauma (1994)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Bickell WH, Wall MJ Jr, Pepe PE, Martin RR, Ginger VF, Allen MK, Mattox KL. Immediate versus delayed fluid resuscitation for hypotensive patients with penetrating torso injuries. N Engl J Med. 1994;331(17):1105-9.
trial_type: Prospective, controlled, single-system prehospital-to-trauma-centre trial; alternate-day (quasi-randomised); unblinded
one_liner: In hypotensive penetrating torso trauma, delaying preoperative crystalloid resuscitation until operative intervention improved survival to hospital discharge compared with immediate fluid aimed at normalising blood pressure.

pico.population: Adults (≥16 years) with penetrating torso injury and prehospital systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg, requiring operative intervention
pico.intervention: Delayed fluid resuscitation: no intravenous fluid bolus before operative intervention; IV access kept patent with minimal flush
pico.comparison: Immediate fluid resuscitation: rapid prehospital and emergency centre isotonic crystalloid infusion targeting systolic blood pressure >100 mm Hg

background.existing_knowledge: In the early 1990s, standard trauma algorithms prioritised rapid restoration of 'normal' blood pressure with large-volume isotonic crystalloid before haemorrhage control in hypotensive trauma.
background.knowledge_gap: Experimental and physiological work raised concern that raising arterial pressure before surgical control could exacerbate ongoing haemorrhage, dislodge early thrombus, and dilute coagulation factors, while prehospital infusion could prolong scene time.
background.hypothesis: In hypotensive patients with penetrating torso injury, delaying preoperative intravenous fluid resuscitation until operative intervention improves survival compared with immediate prehospital and emergency-centre fluid resuscitation.

methods.design: Prospective, controlled, single-system prehospital-to-trauma-centre trial; alternate-day (even/odd day of month) assignment (quasi-randomised); unblinded.
methods.setting: City of Houston EMS system and Ben Taub General Hospital (Baylor College of Medicine) trauma care pathway (prehospital, emergency centre, operating theatre).

inclusion: Penetrating injury to the torso (chest/abdomen/neck or groin exploration as operative indications)
Prehospital systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg (including 'no measurable blood pressure') at initial on-scene assessment
exclusion: Revised Trauma Score (RTS) of 0 at the scene
Fatal gunshot wound to the head
Minor injuries not requiring operative intervention (excluded from analytic cohort)

methods.intervention: Immediate-resuscitation group: standard paramedical protocol plus rapid infusion of isotonic crystalloid (Ringer’s acetate) in the prehospital setting and continued crystalloid infusion in the emergency centre for systolic blood pressure >100 mm Hg (plus packed red cells when necessary per standard criteria). Intraoperative management (both groups): once in theatre and under general anaesthesia, intravenous crystalloid and packed red cells were given as needed to maintain systolic arterial pressure ~100 mm Hg, haematocrit ≥25%, and urine output ≥50 mL/hour; hetastarch occasionally used as additional intravascular volume expander.
methods.comparison: Delayed-resuscitation group: identical clinical pathway except no intravenous fluid bolus/resuscitation before operative intervention. Intravenous access was established prehospital; catheters were capped and flushed with 1–2 mL of 1% heparin in normal saline; any additional emergency-centre catheters were kept patent with Ringer’s acetate at 10 mL/hour (line patency rather than resuscitation). Intraoperative resuscitation targets were the same as the intervention group after arrival in theatre.
methods.blinding: None (prehospital and in-hospital staff were necessarily aware of fluid strategy; primary outcome was objective).
methods.sample_size_power: A priori sample size planned at ~600 patients to detect a 10–15 percentage-point improvement in survival (assuming 35% mortality with standard preoperative fluid resuscitation), with two-sided α=0.05 and β=0.20 (80% power); one interim analysis used a stringent Haybittle–Peto boundary.

headline_bullets: Delayed resuscitation improved survival to discharge: 70% vs 62% (P=0.04).
The intervention created large, clinically meaningful separation in preoperative crystalloid exposure (prehospital 870 vs 92 mL; trauma centre 1608 vs 283 mL; both P<0.001).

Immediate fluids increased systolic BP at arrival (79 vs 72 mm Hg; P=0.02) but were associated with markedly prolonged prothrombin time (14.1 vs 11.4 sec; P<0.001), supporting a plausible harm pathway.

outcomes_table.outcome: Crystalloid before trauma-centre arrival (Ringer’s acetate; mL)
Crystalloid in trauma centre (Ringer’s acetate; mL)
outcomes_table.note: Delayed group received small volumes despite 'no resuscitation' (contamination/rescue not fully described)

outcomes_table.outcome: Packed red cells in trauma centre (mL)
outcomes_table.note: Greater preoperative transfusion requirement in immediate group

outcomes_table.outcome: Systolic BP on trauma-centre arrival (mm Hg)
outcomes_table.note: Physiological effect of early fluid, without translating into improved survival
Pattern consistent with dilutional coagulopathy / haemostatic impairment at presentation
Suggests more aggressive/urgent volume replacement intraoperatively in immediate group

outcomes_table.outcome: Length of hospital stay (days; operative survivors)
outcomes_table.note: Calculated among operative survivors (227 vs 238); ICU stay did not differ (8 ± 16 vs 7 ± 11; P=0.30)

safety: Postoperative complication rate (operative survivors): 30% (immediate) vs 23% (delayed), P=0.08
Adult respiratory distress syndrome (operative survivors): 4% (immediate) vs 1% (delayed), P=0.11

domains.notes: Assignment by even/odd day of month (alternate-day) was pragmatic but not truly random; allocation concealment was not possible, raising risk of selection and performance bias.
Unblinded delivery; prehospital and in-hospital staff were necessarily aware of fluid strategy.

1069 consecutive hypotensive penetrating torso trauma patients were screened; 172 with RTS=0 and 299 with minor injuries not requiring operation were excluded from outcome analysis, leaving 598 analysed (309 immediate; 289 delayed). Exclusions after initial screening can introduce bias if exclusions differ by group. Analyses reported as intention-to-treat by assigned group.

Strong separation in the primary exposure (prehospital Ringer’s acetate 870 ± 667 mL vs 92 ± 309 mL; trauma-centre Ringer’s acetate 1608 ± 1201 vs 283 ± 722 mL). The delayed group still received non-trivial prehospital/trauma-centre fluid on average (92 mL and 283 mL respectively), implying some protocol leakage; the magnitude, indications, and timing of these deviations are not fully granular.
Groups were broadly comparable (age 31 ± 11 vs 31 ± 10 years; male 88% vs 91%; SBP at scene 58 ± 35 vs 59 ± 34 mm Hg; Injury Severity Score 26 ± 14 in both; gunshot wounds 65% vs 67%).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate. The exposure separation and objective primary outcome support credibility, but alternate-day (non-concealed) assignment, lack of blinding, and analytic exclusions after screening increase susceptibility to bias and confounding.

domains.notes: Predominantly young, male, urban penetrating trauma with short prehospital intervals (response ~8 minutes; transport ~12 minutes); applicability strongest to similar systems and injury patterns.

Findings may not translate to rural/prolonged transport settings where longer 'no fluid' intervals could be harmful, particularly if delays to haemorrhage control are substantial. The trial informs penetrating torso haemorrhage without emphasis on traumatic brain injury (TBI); permissive hypotension is typically inappropriate when cerebral perfusion is threatened. Conducted before modern damage-control resuscitation norms (early balanced blood products, tranexamic acid, widespread point-of-care coagulation testing, and prehospital blood components), limiting direct extrapolation to contemporary haemostatic strategies.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate. Highly applicable to short-transport penetrating torso haemorrhage in systems similar to the study setting, but generalisability is limited for blunt trauma, TBI, prolonged prehospital times, and contemporary blood-component resuscitation pathways.

strengths: Large cohort for a prehospital trauma trial
Pragmatic implementation across an entire EMS/trauma pathway
Strong protocol separation in preoperative fluid exposure
Physiologically coherent laboratory differences supportive of mechanism
limitations: Potential confounding by operational factors (e.g., scene time)
Fluid strategy tested was 'near-zero' versus targeting SBP >100 mm Hg (not a modern 'controlled resuscitation' target)

critical_appraisal.summary: A landmark but methodologically limited trial that provided high-profile clinical evidence supporting delayed/controlled resuscitation until haemostasis in penetrating torso haemorrhage, though the quasi-randomised design and era-specific fluid targets limit direct application to modern damage-control resuscitation.
strengths: Large cohort for a prehospital trauma trial
Pragmatic implementation across an entire EMS/trauma pathway
Strong protocol separation in preoperative fluid exposure
Physiologically coherent laboratory differences supportive of mechanism
weaknesses: Potential confounding by operational factors (e.g., scene time)
Fluid strategy tested was 'near-zero' versus targeting SBP >100 mm Hg (not a modern 'controlled resuscitation' target)

sections.authors_conclusion: Delayed preoperative fluid resuscitation improved survival to hospital discharge compared with immediate fluid resuscitation in hypotensive patients with penetrating torso injuries.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial reshaped trauma resuscitation by providing a clinically grounded rationale for permissive hypotension and avoidance of excessive crystalloid prior to haemostasis in penetrating torso trauma with rapid access to definitive haemorrhage control.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Hypotensive penetrating torso trauma in systems with short prehospital transport times and rapid access to operative intervention.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: All trauma patients should have fluids withheld. This does not apply to patients with traumatic brain injury or those with prolonged transport times where permissive hypotension could be harmful.
implementation_caveats: Contemporary permissive hypotension typically targets lower pressures (e.g., SBP ~80–90) in patients without TBI, suggesting the trial may demonstrate harm from over-resuscitation rather than harm from 'any fluid'.
Modern damage-control resuscitation prioritises early balanced blood products and haemostatic resuscitation over crystalloid, a strategy not tested in this trial.

controversies.notes: Alternate-day assignment without concealment and unblinded delivery create risk of systematic differences between groups (including operational behaviours); the modest absolute survival difference (8 percentage points) could be vulnerable to residual confounding even with similar baseline severity.

The delayed group had a shorter scene interval (7 ± 6 vs 9 ± 8 minutes), so part of the observed benefit could plausibly relate to faster transport/earlier haemorrhage control rather than the fluid exposure alone.

Subsequent controlled/hypotensive resuscitation trials in haemorrhagic shock did not consistently reproduce a mortality benefit and often focused on different targets/settings (e.g., ED SBP 70 vs 100).

Meta-analysis of hypotensive resuscitation strategies suggests potential reductions in mortality and transfusion requirements, but heterogeneity of targets, injury patterns, and resuscitation era limits certainty and generalisability.

Contemporary major-haemorrhage trauma guidelines/protocols broadly support avoiding excessive crystalloid and using permissive hypotension until haemorrhage control in patients without suspected TBI, embedding Bickell’s core principle while shifting focus towards balanced blood-component and haemostatic resuscitation.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal blood pressure target for permissive hypotension in penetrating trauma?
How does delayed crystalloid resuscitation compare to early balanced blood product resuscitation in modern trauma systems?
What is the safe duration of permissive hypotension before harm occurs from prolonged hypoperfusion?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In hypotensive penetrating torso trauma with rapid access to haemorrhage control, delaying preoperative crystalloid improves survival—a foundational principle for modern permissive hypotension strategies.
